# Introduction: 

For my project, I’m using the mxmh survey dataset, which has 736 responses and 33 columns. The data includes things like age, favorite genre, hours spent listening to music each day, and whether people listen while working. It also 
has mental health information such as anxiety, depression, insomnia, and OCD scores, plus whether people feel music improves, worsens, or has no effect on their mood.

This dataset is useful because it connects music habits with mental health and focus. That means I can look at questions like: do certain genres (like lo‑fi,pop, or rap) relate to lower anxiety? Does listening while working help people focus? Or does the tempo (BPM) of music make a difference in how people feel?

#Background

Music and Emotional Regulation

Music engages brain reward pathways, releasing dopamine and reducing stress and anxiety. As the Healthline article explains, listening to preferred music can boost motivation and pleasure, though certain genres may reinforce depressive moods when listeners are already vulnerable. This dual effect highlights the complexity of music’s role in mental health.

Cognition, Identity, and Clinical Applications

The Home Monitor on Psychology article emphasizes music’s role in cognition and identity. Research shows that self‑selected music strongly activates reward circuits tied to personal values, explaining its deep emotional impact. Clinical applications include neurologic music therapy, which has been used to restore speech and movement in patients with brain injuries. Studies also show music can regulate memory, imagination, and cultural identity, making it a powerful tool for psychological health.

# Distribution of Favorite Genres

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(mxmh_survey_results, aes(x = `Fav genre`)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Counts of Favorite Genres",
       x = "Genre",
       y = "Count") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```
We can see that rock is the most common favorite genre, followed by Pop and Metal, while Gospel and Latin have the fewest responses.This shows which genres are most popular in the dataset.


# Average Anxiety Score by Genre

```{r}
mxmh_survey_results %>%
  group_by(`Fav genre`) %>%
  summarise(mean_anxiety = mean(Anxiety, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `Fav genre`, y = mean_anxiety)) +
  geom_col(fill = "purple") +
  labs(title = "Average Anxiety Score by Genre",
       x = "Genre",
       y = "Mean Anxiety") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

 Folk listeners reported the highest average anxiety scores, while Latin listeners reported the lowest. This suggests that certain genres may be linked with higher or lower levels of anxiety.

# Depression by Genre 
```{r}
mxmh_survey_results %>%
  group_by(`Fav genre`) %>%
  summarise(mean_depression = mean(Depression, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `Fav genre`, y = mean_depression)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkred") +
  labs(title = "Average Depression Score by Genre",
       x = "Genre",
       y = "Mean Depression") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```
This chart shows that lo‑fi, hip hop, and EDM(electronic dance music) listeners report higher average depression scores, while gospel and Latin music  listeners report the lowest. The chart suggests certain genres may be linked with higher or lower depression levels.


# Using median instead of mean for the visuals 

Anxiety by genre (using meadian)
```{r}
mxmh_survey_results %>%
  group_by(`Fav genre`) %>%
  summarise(median_anxiety = median(Anxiety, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `Fav genre`, y = median_anxiety)) +
  geom_col(fill = "purple") +
  labs(title = "Median Anxiety Score by Genre",
       x = "Genre",
       y = "Median Anxiety") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

Using the median instead of the mean gives a clearer picture of the typical listener’s anxiety level, since it reduces the influence of extreme outliers. Compared to the mean chart, small differences appear: genres like Rock and Lofi show higher median anxiety than their mean suggested, while Rap shows lower. This indicates that outliers were affecting the averages, and the median provides a more reliable summary of how anxiety varies across genres.



#Depression by genre (using median)
```{r}
mxmh_survey_results %>%
  group_by(`Fav genre`) %>%
  summarise(median_depression = median(Depression, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `Fav genre`, y = median_depression)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkred") +
  labs(title = "Median Depression Score by Genre",
       x = "Genre",
       y = "Median Depression") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

```

Switching from mean to median highlights some differences in how genres compare. Lofi listeners show the highest median depression scores, even higher than their mean suggested, while Gospel and Latin remain the lowest. Hip hop stays high, but the median chart makes Lofi stand out more clearly as the top. This shows that extreme values were influencing the averages, and the median provides a more representative summary of typical scores across genres.



#Distributions of Quantative Variables


#Age distribution

```{r}
ggplot(mxmh_survey_results, aes(x = Age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Age Distribution", x = "Age", y = "Count")

ggplot(mxmh_survey_results, aes(y = Age)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Age Boxplot", y = "Age")
```

The age distribution is right‑skewed, with most participants between 20–30 years old and a clear peak near 25. Counts steadily decrease as age increases, with very few respondents above 60.

The boxplot confirms this skew, showing the interquartile range centered in the mid‑20s and numerous outliers extending into older ages. This suggests the dataset is dominated by younger participants, while older ages appear as outliers that pull the mean upward compared to the median.



#Hours per Day Listenting to music 
```{r}
ggplot(mxmh_survey_results, aes(x = `Hours per day`)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "purple") +
  labs(title = "Hours per Day Distribution", x = "Hours per Day", y = "Count")

ggplot(mxmh_survey_results, aes(y = `Hours per day`)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "purple") +
  labs(title = "Hours per Day Boxplot", y = "Hours per Day")

```
The distribution is right‑skewed, with most participants listening between 1–5 hours daily and a clear peak around 2–3 hours. 
The boxplot shows the interquartile range centered in this range, with the median near 3 hours. Several extreme outliers appear above 10 hours, extending up to 25, which pull the mean upward compared to the median. This indicates that while typical listening behavior is moderate, a small group of heavy listeners significantly increases the spread.

```{r}
ggplot(mxmh_survey_results,
       aes(x = factor(`Hours per day`))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "purple") +
  labs(title = "Hours per Day Responses",
       x = "Hours per Day",
       y = "Count")
```
The bar chart shows the exact values participants reported for hours spent listening to music each day. Most responses clustered around 1, 2, 3, and 4 hours, with 2 hours being the most common response. The gaps between many decimal values suggest that participants tended to report rounded estimates rather than precise listening times.


#Anxiety Distribution
```{r}
ggplot(mxmh_survey_results, aes(x = Anxiety)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "orange") +
  labs(title = "Anxiety Score Distribution", x = "Anxiety Score", y = "Count")

ggplot(mxmh_survey_results, aes(y = Anxiety)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "orange") +
  labs(title = "Anxiety Score Boxplot", y = "Anxiety Score")


```
Distribution: The anxiety distribution is left‑skewed, with most participants reporting scores between 6 and 9. The tallest bars appear around 7–8, showing that higher anxiety scores are more common in this dataset. Lower scores (0–3) occur much less frequently, creating a long tail on the left side. This pattern suggests that the sample overall tends toward moderate to high anxiety levels.

Box plot:
The boxplot shows the median anxiety score around 6, with the middle 50% of scores (IQR) ranging roughly from 4 to 8. The whiskers extend from 0 to 10, indicating the full range of responses. There are no extreme outliers, but the wide spread shows substantial variability in anxiety levels across participants. The higher concentration of values in the upper quartile aligns with the histogram’s peak around 7–8. 



#Depression Distribution
```{r}
ggplot(mxmh_survey_results, aes(x = Depression)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "darkred") +
  labs(title = "Depression Score Distribution", x = "Depression Score", y = "Count")

ggplot(mxmh_survey_results, aes(y = Depression)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "darkred") +
  labs(title = "Depression Score Boxplot", y = "Depression Score")
```
Distribution: The depression distribution is multi‑modal, meaning it has several peaks rather than one clear dominant range. You can see noticeable clusters around 0–2 and again around 7–8, showing that participants tend to fall into either lower or higher depression score groups. Middle scores (3–5) appear less frequent, creating a dip in the center of the distribution. This pattern suggests the dataset contains two distinct groups: one with low depression symptoms and another with higher levels.

Box Plot: The boxplot shows the median depression score around 5, with the interquartile range stretching from roughly 2.5 to 7.5. This wide IQR indicates substantial variability in depression levels across the sample. The whiskers extend across the full range (0–10), and there are no extreme outliers, meaning the variation is part of the natural spread of responses. The boxplot’s wide middle section aligns with the histogram’s two clusters, showing that depression scores are not centered around a single typical value.




#Insomnia Distribution
```{r}

ggplot(mxmh_survey_results, aes(x = Insomnia)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "skyblue") +
  labs(title = "Insomnia Score Distribution", x = "Insomnia Score", y = "Count")

ggplot(mxmh_survey_results, aes(y = Insomnia)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "skyblue") +
  labs(title = "Insomnia Score Boxplot", y = "Insomnia Score")
```
Distribution: The insomnia distribution is strongly right‑skewed, with the highest concentration of scores at 0. The count drops steadily as insomnia scores increase, showing that most participants report little to no insomnia symptoms. Higher scores (7–10) appear much less frequently, forming a long tail on the right side. This pattern suggests that insomnia is not widespread in the dataset, but a smaller group of participants experiences more severe symptoms.

Box plot:  The boxplot shows the median insomnia score around 3, with the interquartile range stretching from roughly 1 to 6. This indicates moderate variability among participants. The whiskers extend across the full range (0–10), showing that while most scores cluster toward the lower end, the dataset includes individuals with severe insomnia. The combination of a low median and a long right tail aligns with the histogram’s strong right skew.



#OCD Distribution

#Anxiety vs Depression by Genre (using median)
```{r}
mxmh_survey_results %>%
  group_by(`Fav genre`) %>%
  summarise(
    median_anxiety = median(Anxiety, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_depression = median(Depression, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(median_anxiety, median_depression),
               names_to = "Measure",
               values_to = "Score") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `Fav genre`, y = Score, fill = Measure)) +
  geom_col(position ="dodge" ) +
  labs(title = "Median Anxiety vs. Depression Score by Genre",
       x = "Genre",
       y = "Median Score") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

This chart compares median anxiety and depression scores side by side for each genre. It shows that some genres, like Lofi and Hip hop, have high median scores for both measures, while Gospel and Latin remain consistently low. Looking at both together highlights which genres are linked with higher or lower levels of mental health concerns, and using the median ensures the results are more representative of typical listeners rather than being skewed by outliers.

#Looking at correlations 

#Anxiety and Insomnia

Scatterplot of Anxiety and Insomnia
```{r}
ggplot(mxmh_survey_results,
       aes(x = Anxiety,
           y = Insomnia)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15,
              height = 0.15,
              alpha = 0.35,
              color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm",se = FALSE, color = "darkred") +
  labs(title = "Anxiety and Insomnia",
       x = "Anxiety Score",
       y = "Insomnia Score")
cor(mxmh_survey_results$Anxiety,
    mxmh_survey_results$Insomnia,
    use = "complete.obs") 
```
```{r}
cor(mxmh_survey_results$Anxiety,
    mxmh_survey_results$Insomnia,
    use="complete.obs")
```

The scatterplot shows a slight upward trend, but the points are widely spread. Together with the correlation of 0.29, this indicates a weak positive relationship, meaning participants with higher anxiety scores tended to report slightly higher insomnia scores, but the relationship was not strong.

#Predicting effect on mood

Before building a model, I first looked at how participants responded to the Music effects

 #Looking at the Music effects groups

```{r}
table(mxmh_survey_results$`Music effects`, useNA = "ifany")
```
Most participants reported that music improved their mood, with 542 responses compared to 169 reporting no effect and only 17 reporting that music worsened their mood. The groups are uneven in size, especially the Worsen group, which is important to consider when comparing the groups and building a prediction model. 



 #Depression Scores by Music effect
 
```{r}
ggplot(mxmh_survey_results,
       aes(x = `Music effects`,
           y = Depression,
           fill = `Music effects`)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Depression Scores by Music Effect",
       x = "Music Effect",
       y = "Depression Score")
```

# Depression scores by Music Effect (excluding missing responses)

```{r}
mxmh_survey_results %>%
  filter(!is.na(`Music effects`)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `Music effects`,
             y = Depression,
             fill = `Music effects`)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Depression Scores by Music Effect",
       x = "Music Effect",
       y = "Depression Score")
```
Depression scores appear to differ across reported music effects. Participants who reported that music worsened their mood had a higher median depression score than those who reported improvement or no effect.


#Depression summary statistics by Music Effect

```{r}
mxmh_survey_results %>%
  filter(!is.na(`Music effects`)) %>%
  group_by(`Music effects`) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    mean_depression = mean(Depression, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_depression = sd(Depression, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_depression = median(Depression, na.rm = TRUE),
    IQR_depression = IQR(Depression, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

Depression scores were highest among participants who reported that music worsened their mood. This group had a median depression score of 8 and a mean of 7.18, compared with a median of 5 for the Improve group and 4 for the No effect group. All three groups had an IQR of 5, but the Worsen group only included 17 participant.


#Depression scores and reported Music Effect (treated as categorical variable)

```{r}
mxmh_survey_results %>%
  filter(!is.na(`Music effects`)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Depression),
             fill = `Music effects`)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(title = "Music Effects by Depression Score",
       x = "Depression Score",
       y = "Proportion",
       fill = "Music Effect")
```

Music improvement was the most common response across nearly all depression scores. The proportion reporting that music worsened their mood appears larger among some of the highest depression scores, especially 9 and 10.

OCD scores look fairly similar across all three music effect groups, with the No effect group showing a slightly lower median. The large amount of overlap suggests that OCD may not strongly distinguish how participants report music affecting their mood.



The box plot shows that anxiety scores vary across the different reported music effects. Participants who reported that music worsens their mood have a median anxiety score of about 7, and those who reported that music improves their mood also have a median around 7. The no effect group has a lower median anxiety score of about 5. Overall, the groups overlap quite a bit, so anxiety scores alone do not clearly separate the music-effect groups.



 #Anxiety summary statistics by Music Effect

```{r}
mxmh_survey_results %>%
  filter(!is.na(`Music effects`)) %>%
  group_by(`Music effects`) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    mean_anxiety = mean(Anxiety, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_anxiety = sd(Anxiety, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_anxiety = median(Anxiety, na.rm = TRUE),
    IQR_anxiety = IQR(Anxiety, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

Anxiety scores were lower among participants who reported that music had no effect on their mood. The No effect group had a median anxiety score of 5, compared with 7 for both the Improve and Worsen groups. The Improve and Worsen groups also had slightly smaller IQRs, although the Worsen group only contained 17 participants and should be interpreted carefully.

 # Anxiety scores by reported music effect( categorical)

```{r}
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Anxiety),

  geom_bar(position = "fill") +

       x = "Anxiety Score",
```

Music improvement was the most common response across most anxiety scores.        y = "Insomnia Score")

The boxplot shows that insomnia scores are very similar for participants who reported that music had no effect and those who reported that music improved their mood. Participants in the Worsen group appear to have slightly higher insomnia scores, although this group contains far fewer participants.


# Insomnia summary statistics by Music Effect

```{r}
mxmh_survey_results %>%
  filter(!is.na(`Music effects`)) %>%
  group_by(`Music effects`) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    mean_insomnia = mean(Insomnia, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_insomnia = sd(Insomnia, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_insomnia = median(Insomnia, na.rm = TRUE),
    IQR_insomnia = IQR(Insomnia, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

Insomnia scores were very similar between participants who reported no effect and those who reported improvement, with both groups having a median of 3 and an IQR of 5. The Worsen group had a slightly higher median of 4, but because this group only includes 17 participants. Overall, insomnia does not appear to separate the music effect groups as clearly as depression or anxiety.

#Insomnia scores by Music Effect(as categories)

```{r}
mxmh_survey_results %>%
  filter(!is.na(`Music effects`)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Insomnia),

  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(title = "Music Effects by Insomnia Score",
       x = "Insomnia Score",
       y = "Proportion",
       fill = "Music Effect")
```

Music improvement was the most common response across nearly all insomnia scores. The proportions were fairly similar across most scores, with no clear increasing or decreasing pattern, suggesting that insomnia may not strongly distinguish participants’ reported music effects.

# Summary of group comparisions
Depression and anxiety showed the clearest differences across the music effect groups. Insomnia and OCD scores were more similar across the groups, suggesting that they may be less useful for predicting participants’ reported music effects. Because the Worsen group only contains 17 participants, all comparisons involving that group should be interpreted carefully.


#Exploring Other Possible Predictors
Before building the model, I looked at other variables that may help predict whether participants report that music improves their mood.

Hours per Day by Music Effect
# Compare listening time across Music Effect groups

```{r}
mxmh_survey_results %>%
  filter(!is.na(`Music effects`)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `Music effects`,
             y = `Hours per day`,
             fill = `Music effects`)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Hours of Music per Day by Music Effect",
       x = "Music Effect",
       y = "Hours per Day")
```
Participants who reported that music improved their mood appear to listen to slightly more music per day, with a median around 3 hours compared with about 2 hours for the No effect and Worsen groups. However, the groups still overlap considerably, so Hours per Day alone may not strongly distinguish reported music effects.

# Hours per Day summary statistics by Music Effect

```{r}
mxmh_survey_results %>%
  filter(!is.na(`Music effects`)) %>%
  group_by(`Music effects`) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    mean_hours = mean(`Hours per day`, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_hours = sd(`Hours per day`, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_hours = median(`Hours per day`, na.rm = TRUE),
    IQR_hours = IQR(`Hours per day`, na.rm = TRUE))
```

Participants who reported that music improved their mood had a slightly higher median listening time of 3 hours per day, compared with 2 hours for both the No effect and Worsen groups. The differences are relatively small and the groups overlap, so Hours per Day may provide some information but does not strongly separate the Music Effect groups by itself.


# While Working and reported Music Effect

```{r}
mxmh_survey_results %>%
  filter(!is.na(`Music effects`),

  ggplot(aes(x = `While working`,

  geom_bar(position = "fill") +

```
Participants who listened to music while working had a noticeably larger proportion reporting that music improved their mood compared with those who did not listen while working. Participants who did not listen while working were more likely to report that music had no effect, suggesting that listening while working may be useful to explore as a predictor of reported music effects.

Music improvement was the most common response across every favorite genre. Some genres appeared to have different proportions of No effect and Worsen responses, but several genre groups had very few participants, so these differences should be interpreted carefully.


#Creating Binary Music Effect Response

To prepare for binary logistic regression, I combined participants who reported No effect or Worsen into one No improvement group, while keeping Improve as its own group.

 #Combine Music Effect into two groups for logistic regression

```{r}
mxmh_survey_results <- mxmh_survey_results %>%
  mutate(
    `Music improvement` = case_when(
      `Music effects` == "Improve" ~ "Improve",
      `Music effects` %in% c("No effect", "Worsen") ~ "No improvement",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )
```
# Check the new response groups
```{r}
table(mxmh_survey_results$`Music improvement`,
      useNA = "ifany")
```
The new response variable contains 542 participants in the Improve group and 186 in the No improvement group, with 8 missing responses. This binary outcome will be used for the logistic regression model.


#Binary Logistic Regression

I started with Depression as the first predictor because Depression showed noticeable differences across the Music Effect groups during the exploratory analysis.

# Set the new response as a factor
```{r}
mxmh_survey_results$`Music improvement` <-
  factor(mxmh_survey_results$`Music improvement`,
         levels = c("No improvement", "Improve"))
```

# First binary logistic regression using Depression
```{r}
model_1 <- glm(
  `Music improvement` ~ Depression,
  data = mxmh_survey_results,
  family = binomial)
summary(model_1)
```
In the first logistic regression model, Depression was not a significant predictor of whether participants reported music improving their mood (p = 0.376).


#Model 2: Adding Anxiety
Since Anxiety also showed differences across the Music improvement groups, I added Anxiety to the Depression model to see whether it provides additional information for predicting reported music improvement.

```{r}
model_2 <- glm(
  `Music improvement` ~ Depression + Anxiety,
  data = mxmh_survey_results,
  family = binomial)
summary(model_2)
```
Model 2 showed that Anxiety was a statistically significant predictor of reported music improvement (p = 0.001), while Depression remained non-significant (p = 0.343). Higher anxiety scores were associated with higher odds of reporting Improve rather than No improvement.

# Model 3: Depression + Anxiety + While Working
Since listening while working showed a noticeable difference in reported music improvement, I added While Working to the Depression and Anxiety model.

```{r}
model_3 <- glm(
  `Music improvement` ~ Depression + Anxiety + `While working`,
  data = mxmh_survey_results,
  family = binomial)
summary(model_3)
```
Model 3 showed that Anxiety and listening while working were statistically significant predictors of reported music improvement. Higher anxiety scores and listening to music while working were associated with higher odds of reporting Improve, while Depression remained non-significant.

#Model 4: Adding Hours per Day
Since Hours per Day showed a small difference across the Music Effect groups, I added it to the model to see whether listening time provides additional information for predicting music improvement.

```{r}
model_4 <- glm( `Music improvement` ~ Depression + Anxiety + `While working` + `Hours per day`,
  data = mxmh_survey_results,
  family = binomial)
summary(model_4)
```
Model 4 showed that Anxiety and listening while working remained statistically significant predictors of reported music improvement. Depression and Hours per Day were not significant, suggesting that listening time did not add much predictive information after accounting for the other variables.

# Comparing the Logistic Regression Models
```{r}
AIC(model_1, model_2, model_3, model_4)
```
Model 3 had a lower AIC than Model 4 (800.62 compared with 802.48), suggesting that adding Hours per Day did not improve the model enough to justify the additional predictor. Combined with its non-significant p-value, this suggests that Hours per Day may not be useful to keep in the final model.


Model 5: Anxiety and Listening While Working
Since Anxiety and While Working remained significant in the previous models, I created a simpler model using only these two predictors.

# Model 5: Anxiety + While Working

```{r}
model_5 <- glm(
  `Music improvement` ~ Anxiety + `While working`,
  data = mxmh_survey_results,
  family = binomial)
summary(model_5)
```
Model 5 showed that Anxiety and listening while working were both statistically significant predictors of reported music improvement. Model 5 also had a slightly lower AIC than Model 3, suggesting that removing Depression created a simpler model without the reducing model fit.

#Comparing Model 3 and Model 5
```{r}
AIC(model_3, model_5)
```

Model 3 and Model 5 had very similar AIC values (800.62 and 800.35). Since Model 5 uses fewer predictors and Depression was not statistically significant in Model 3, Model 5 provides a simpler model with similar fit.


#Training and Testing the Models
Before fitting the final prediction models, I created a separate modeling dataset using the regrouped Music improvement response. 

# Creating the modeling dataset
```{r}
model_data <- mxmh_survey_results %>%
  filter(!is.na(`Music improvement`))
table(model_data$`Music improvement`)
```
The modeling dataset contains 542 participants in the Improve group and 186 participants in the No improvement group, for a total of 728 participants.

80/20 Training and Testing Split
# Split modeling data into 80% training and 20% testing
```{r}
set.seed(123)
train_index <- sample(
  1:nrow(model_data),
  size = 0.80 * nrow(model_data))

train_data <- model_data[train_index, ]

test_data <- model_data[-train_index, ]
# Check training and testing sizes

nrow(train_data)
nrow(test_data)

table(train_data$`Music improvement`)
table(test_data$`Music improvement`)
```
The cleaned modeling data were randomly split into 582 training observations and 146 testing observations, using approximately 80% of the data for model development and 20% for evaluating predictions on unseen observations.


# Full logistic model using training data only

```{r}
full_model <- glm(
  `Music improvement` ~ Age + `Hours per day` + `While working` +
    `Fav genre` + Anxiety + Depression + Insomnia + OCD,
  data = train_data,
  family = binomial
)

summary(full_model)
```
In the full training model, Anxiety and listening while working were statistically significant predictors of reported music improvement. Age, Hours per Day, Depression, Insomnia, OCD, and Favorite Genre did not show clear individual effects in this model.

Backward Selection
Some predictor variables contained missing values, so I created a complete version of the training data to make sure each model being compared used the same participants.

```{r}
train_complete <- train_data %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(Age),
    !is.na(`Hours per day`),
    !is.na(`While working`),
    !is.na(`Fav genre`),
    !is.na(Anxiety),
    !is.na(Depression),
    !is.na(Insomnia),
    !is.na(OCD)
  )

nrow(train_complete)
```
# Refit full model using complete training data

```{r} 
full_model_complete <- glm(
  `Music improvement` ~ Age + `Hours per day` + `While working` +
    `Fav genre` + Anxiety + Depression + Insomnia + OCD,
  data = train_complete,
  family = binomial
)
# Perform backward selection

backward_model <- step(
  full_model_complete,
  direction = "backward"
)

summary(backward_model)
```

Backward selection reduced the full training model to Anxiety and Listening While Working. Both predictors remained statistically significant, suggesting that these two variables provided the most useful information for predicting reported music improvement among the predictors included in the full model.


# Keep complete test observations for the final model

```{r}
test_complete <- test_data %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(Anxiety),
    !is.na(`While working`))

nrow(test_complete)
```

# Predict probabilities

```{r}
test_prob <- predict(
  backward_model,
  newdata = test_complete,
  type = "response")
```

# Convert probabilities into predicted groups

```{r}
test_prediction <- ifelse(
  test_prob >= 0.50,
  "Improve",
  "No improvement")
```
# Confusion matrix

```{r}
confusion_matrix <- table(
  Predicted = test_prediction,
  Actual = test_complete$`Music improvement`)

confusion_matrix
```
# Accuracy
```{r}
accuracy <- mean(
  test_prediction == test_complete$`Music improvement`)

accuracy
```
The backward-selected model had an overall test accuracy of 72.4%. However, the confusion matrix showed that the model predicted Improve for almost every participant and correctly identified only 1 of the 41 actual No improvement cases. This suggests that overall accuracy alone overstates the model's predictive ability because the outcome groups are imbalanced.
